name: Zoe Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Bryce's Farm for Mr Bryce, who's eighty-two and a widower with no children. It's two hundred hectares of wheat, barley and field beans, and eighty suckler cows with their calves. I'm up at six, feed round first, then I'm either on the drill or the sprayer, or doing the books in the farm office, and on Sundays I'm church warden at St Michael's in the village.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love drilling in autumn, when the field's ready and the seed goes in straight. Mr Bryce has hinted for years that he'd like me to take the farm on one day, and that keeps me going. What wears me out is the money in the meantime: Ben, my husband, drives for the grain merchant, I'm on a farmworker's wage with a manager's job, and with Ellie and Tom and the mortgage, a broken boiler would sink us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought: helpful for the forms and not much else. I use one of those AI programs now and then for the grant applications, and it saves me a Sunday afternoon. On the farm itself, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's fine for me. Things stay steady, Mr Bryce stays in charge, and I keep hoping he'll put something in writing about the farm. AI doesn't change that one way or the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Mr Bryce, gently, to sit down with a solicitor about the future of the farm. I'd keep using the AI for forms and maybe try it for the cattle records too. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, mostly, apart from the usual money worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to you to take the farm on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. I'd be the first woman in my family to farm in her own name. My grandfather was a cowman all his life and never owned so much as a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked Mr Bryce for it in writing before now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it feels grasping, asking an old man about his will. My mother taught me you don't do that. But I know I should.

S0.say: It's what I thought: helpful for the forms and not much else. I use an AI program now and then for grant applications, but on the farm nothing changes.
S0.think: It's fine for me. Things stay steady, and I keep hoping Mr Bryce will put something in writing about the farm, which AI doesn't change.
S0.do: Keeps managing the farm and gently asks the owner to meet a solicitor about its future. Keeps using AI for grant forms and tries it for the cattle records.
S0.feel: Calm and mostly settled, apart from the usual money worries.
S0.quote: My grandfather was a cowman all his life and never owned so much as a field.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe's hope of one day farming in her own name shapes everything she says. She's comfortable using AI for paperwork without making much of it. Her reluctance to ask the owner about his will comes from her upbringing, and she knows it's holding her back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms will need to change, and good farms will change carefully. I'd say young people should get apprenticeships to run the new kit, not just be told to go to university. That's what I'd tell the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about two things. If the farm needs expensive robots to stay in business, Mr Bryce might decide to sell instead of handing it on. And Ben's lorry job could go to self-driving trucks before mine goes at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first robot tractors to prove themselves on a few farms nearby, then I'd look at the numbers. I'd push Mr Bryce on the solicitor meeting sooner. And I'd start putting fifty a month into a savings account, which we've never managed, so we've something if Ben's hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but more watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben, first. Then the vicar, honestly, he's wise about these things. And the other farmers at the machinery ring, because they'll know what's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I'd seen them work for others. Probably for the crop planning and the cattle records. I'd be a bit behind, but I'd catch up.

S1.say: Farms need to change, and good farms change carefully. Young people should get apprenticeships to run the new kit, not just be told to go to university.
S1.think: I'd worry Mr Bryce might sell rather than hand on a farm that needs expensive robots. And Ben's lorry job could go to self-driving trucks before mine goes at all.
S1.do: Waits for robot tractors to prove themselves on nearby farms before looking at the numbers. Pushes the owner for a solicitor meeting sooner and starts saving fifty a month in case her husband's hours drop.
S1.feel: Uneasy and more watchful, but not frightened.
S1.quote: Ben's lorry job could go to self-driving trucks before mine goes at all.
S1.fieldNote: Her worries in this picture are two steps removed from her own skills: the owner's decision and her husband's driving job. She's a typical careful adopter, waiting for proof from the machinery ring. She'd go to her husband and the vicar before anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too much too fast, and that communities will have to pull together. I'd say families and churches need to look after people who lose their work. And I'd say I'm not one for government handouts, but this is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think Mr Bryce would sell. He's eighty-two, and if someone offered him good money for land to run with robots, he'd take it and I wouldn't blame him. And if Ben's driving goes at the same time, we've nothing coming in at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask Mr Bryce straight out what he plans, no more tiptoeing. We'd cut back to the mortgage, food and heat. I'd ask at the agricultural merchants and the auction mart for any work going, and I'd go to the church's hardship fund if we had to, though it'd hurt my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like everything I'd hoped for was being taken off the table before I'd had a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellie and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right, because we have each other and the church. Ellie's fourteen and she'd want the details, so I'd give her some. Tom's eleven, he'd only care about the calves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for handouts, but you'd use the hardship fund. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not a handout if it's your own community, it's neighbours. I'd pay it back, and I'd help the next family. That's the difference.

S2.say: This is too much too fast, and communities will have to pull together, with families and churches looking after those who lose work. I'm not one for government handouts, but this is different.
S2.think: I think Mr Bryce would sell to someone running robots, and I wouldn't blame him. If Ben's driving goes at the same time, we've nothing coming in at all.
S2.do: Asks the owner directly what he plans for the farm, without tiptoeing. Cuts spending to mortgage, food and heat, looks for work at the merchants and auction mart, and turns to the church hardship fund if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, as if everything she'd hoped for was being taken away before she had a chance.
S2.quote: It's not a handout if it's your own community, it's neighbours. I'd pay it back, and I'd help the next family.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens her hope of taking on the farm more than her current job. She resolved the gap between her views on handouts and using the church fund clearly and without defensiveness. A double hit to both incomes is what makes this alarming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for farms to plan if they start now. I'd tell the young farmers' club to get practical training on the new kit, apprenticeships, not just apps on a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years gives me a chance at the farm. If Mr Bryce agreed a handover, I could bring in the robots myself and make it pay. But I'd be borrowing with nothing behind me, and that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get the handover agreed in writing with a solicitor. I'd do a short course on running robot tractors once others at the machinery ring had done it. I'd keep saving the fifty a month, and Ben would look at retraining as a mechanic for the new trucks, because they'll still need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful too. It's a race, but one I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years Mr Bryce sells and I'm out. With five, I've time to show him I can run it with the new kit. And I can get the paperwork done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for robots with almost no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd share them through the machinery ring, the way we already share a combine. And I'd go to the bank with a plan. I won't pretend I'm sure they'd say yes.

S3.say: Five years is enough for farms to plan if they start now. Young farmers should get practical training and apprenticeships on the new kit, not just apps on a phone.
S3.think: Five years gives me a chance at the farm, because with a handover I could bring in robots myself and make it pay. But I'd be borrowing with nothing behind me, and that frightens me.
S3.do: Gets a farm handover agreed in writing with a solicitor in the first year and takes a robot tractor course once others in the machinery ring have. Keeps saving, plans to share robots through the ring, and supports her husband retraining as a truck mechanic.
S3.feel: Anxious but hopeful, like a race she could win.
S3.quote: With two years Mr Bryce sells and I'm out. With five, I've time to show him I can run it with the new kit.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the threat into a chance to take on the farm, which is her deepest hope. She'd still wait for peers before training, true to her steady style. The fear is borrowing with no savings, and she's honest she can't promise the bank would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this properly. Farms should be handed on to people who'll work them, and apprenticeships should teach the new kit. I'd say it at church and at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. By 2036 I could have the farm in my name, with machines doing the hard work and me making the decisions. The kids would be grown and Ben would have had time to change trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the handover agreed with Mr Bryce in the first year or two, and do the robot course once it was proven. I'd bring in one robot at a time, starting with a weeder for the beans. And I'd keep saving and pay the car loan off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a quiet way. More hope than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots do the decisions too, by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd want to own the farm anyway. Whoever owns the land still decides what it's for. That's the bit I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Bryce changing his mind, or not living long enough to sign. That's the thing I lie awake about, not the robots.

S4.say: Ten years is time to do this properly. Farms should be handed on to people who'll work them, and apprenticeships should teach the new kit.
S4.think: I think I'd be all right. By 2036 I could have the farm in my name with machines doing the hard work, the kids grown and Ben in a new trade.
S4.do: Agrees the handover with the owner in the first year or two and takes the robot course once it's proven. Brings in robots one at a time, starting with a bean weeder, and keeps saving and clears the car loan.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a quiet way, with more hope than fear.
S4.quote: Whoever owns the land still decides what it's for. That's the bit I want.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she sees AGI as something she can use, provided she owns the land. Her real fear is the owner's health or a change of heart, not technology. Her focus on ownership fits her traditional, free-market views.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Mr Bryce would sell and Ben's job would go at the same time. What would help is proper rules that make it easier to hand farms to the people who work them, and apprenticeships so people like Ben and my kids can learn the new trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the church, or the village. If farms go to robots, the villages empty out, and then who fills the pews, who runs the young farmers? That's what worries me past my own job.

headlineQuote: If farms go to robots, the villages empty out, and then who fills the pews, who runs the young farmers?
portrait: Zoe Quinn is a 43-year-old farm manager for an elderly widower with no heirs, running cereals, beans and suckler cows, a church warden who hopes one day to farm in her own name. She uses AI now and then for forms and adopts new kit once neighbours have proven it. She's calm in the hype picture and uneasy in the steady one, worried mainly that the owner might sell and her husband's lorry job might go. A two-year AGI arrival alarms her because both would happen at once, but with five or ten years she sees a path to taking on the farm and using robots herself.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because the owner would sell the farm and her husband's driving job would go at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making it easier to hand farms to the people who work them, and apprenticeships so her husband and children can learn new trades.
